title: Cedar vs Pressure-Treated Decks: How Staining Differs
metaDescription: Cedar and pressure-treated decks need different cleaning and staining approaches. Here is what actually changes between the two and why it matters.
excerpt: Cedar and pressure-treated lumber respond to stain differently. Here is what changes in the cleaning, sanding, and finishing process between the two wood types.
heroAlt: Side by side comparison of cedar decking and pressure-treated decking before staining in a Southwestern Ontario backyard
keyTakeaways: Cedar and pressure-treated lumber are the two most common deck materials across Kitchener-Waterloo, and each needs a slightly different approach to cleaning, sanding, and staining.
Pressure-treated wood can raise a fuzzy grain after sanding and often holds moisture longer, which affects how soon it is ready to stain.
Cedar is softer, more prone to UV greying, and generally accepts penetrating oil-based stain more readily once properly cleaned.

body.text: Most decks across Kitchener, Waterloo, Cambridge, and the wider Southwestern Ontario region are built from one of two materials: pressure-treated lumber or cedar. They can look similar once stained, but they are genuinely different woods with different cell structures, different moisture behaviour, and different reactions to cleaning and sanding. Treating them identically during a staining project is one of the more common shortcuts that leads to disappointing results. This guide breaks down what actually changes between the two and why Restore My Deck approaches them differently rather than applying a single standard process to every job.
Why the wood type matters before you even pick a stain

It is easy to focus on stain colour and finish level, transparent, semi-transparent, semi-solid, or solid, and skip past the more foundational question of what the deck is actually built from. Stain performance depends heavily on how well it penetrates the wood fibre, and pressure-treated lumber and cedar absorb finish differently because of how each is structured and, in the case of pressure-treated wood, chemically processed. Getting the prep work right for the specific material is what determines whether a stain job looks even and lasts the expected 2 to 4 years before needing a refresh, or fails early in blotchy patches.
Pressure-treated decks: what makes them different

Pressure-treated lumber is treated with preservative chemicals under pressure to resist rot and insect damage, which is why it dominates new deck construction. That treatment process affects staining in a few specific ways. First, pressure-treated wood often retains moisture longer than cedar, particularly if it is relatively new, and staining wood that has not dried sufficiently can trap moisture under the finish and cause peeling. Second, sanding pressure-treated lumber tends to raise a slightly fuzzy grain rather than a smooth surface, since the treatment process can affect how the wood fibres respond to abrasion. That fuzz needs to be addressed properly during the 80-grit buff sanding stage so the stain lays down evenly rather than catching on raised fibres.

Older pressure-treated decks, meanwhile, often carry a build-up of mildew, algae, or greying that needs a thorough eco-friendly, plant-safe cleaning pass before sanding even begins. This is especially common on shaded decks or those close to mature trees, both of which are common across established Kitchener-Waterloo neighbourhoods.
Cedar decks: what makes them different

Cedar is a softer wood, naturally more resistant to rot and insects than most species, which is part of why it has long been a popular choice for custom decks and older builds across this region. Because it is softer, cedar can be more sensitive to aggressive power washing, which is one reason the choice between power washing and gentler soft washing is tailored to the wood rather than applied uniformly. Cedar is also more prone to visible UV greying over time, since sun exposure breaks down the surface fibres and lifts the wood's natural oils, leaving a silvery, weathered look on decks that have gone a few years without maintenance.

The upside is that once properly cleaned and sanded, cedar tends to accept a penetrating oil-based stain readily, often producing a rich, even colour that showcases the wood's natural grain particularly well under transparent and semi-transparent finishes. That is part of why semi-transparent stain, the most requested option across our service area, tends to look especially good on well-maintained cedar.

If you are not sure whether your deck is cedar or pressure-treated, that is a completely normal question to ask when requesting a quote. It is one of the first things assessed, whether from photos or an on-site visit, since it shapes the entire prep process.
How the cleaning step changes

Cleaning is not a one-size-fits-all step. Pressure-treated wood generally tolerates a firmer power washing approach, though pressure and technique are still adjusted based on the board's age and condition to avoid gouging the surface. Cedar, being softer, more often calls for soft washing, a gentler cleaning method that uses lower pressure combined with the same eco-friendly, plant-safe solutions to lift dirt and mildew without damaging the wood fibre. Choosing the wrong cleaning method for the wood type is a common cause of surface damage that then has to be corrected during sanding, adding time and cost that a properly matched process would have avoided.
How the sanding step changes

The 80-grit buff sanding that precedes every stain job serves the same basic purpose on both wood types: opening the grain so the stain can penetrate rather than sit on the surface. But the technique differs. Pressure-treated wood's tendency to raise fuzzy grain means sanding sometimes needs a follow-up pass to knock down fibres that lift during the first sanding session. Cedar sands more predictably but requires a lighter touch in spots where the wood has softened or where old finish has worn unevenly, since over-sanding soft cedar can create low spots that show through the finished stain.
How the staining step changes

By the time a deck reaches the staining stage, most of the wood-specific work has already happened during cleaning and sanding, but the application still accounts for differences in absorption rate. Restore My Deck uses premium penetrating oil-based stains, including Ready Seal and Penofin Verde, brush-applied rather than sprayed so the finish is worked into the wood rather than laid on top of it. Cedar tends to absorb stain more evenly once properly prepped, often producing a richer, more consistent tone. Pressure-treated wood can absorb unevenly in spots where the original treatment process varied, which is one reason a careful, brush-applied technique matters more on pressure-treated decks than it would with a sprayed application that cannot compensate for those variations as easily.
Which wood type is more common locally, and why it matters

Across Kitchener, Waterloo, Cambridge, Guelph, and the surrounding towns, pressure-treated lumber tends to dominate newer construction, while cedar shows up more often on older homes, custom builds, and higher-end decks built before pressure-treated lumber became the standard choice. Knowing which category your deck falls into is useful before you even request a quote, since it gives a rough sense of what the prep process will involve and roughly how the finished product should look. If your deck combines materials, which does happen on decks that have had partial rebuilds or added features like pergolas or built-in benches, that mixed construction is worth mentioning up front so the quote accounts for handling both wood types correctly.
Getting the right process for your specific deck

The bottom line is that a deck staining process built for cedar and one built for pressure-treated lumber are not interchangeable, even though the end goal, a clean, evenly stained, protected surface, looks the same. Restore My Deck's four-step process, clean, repair, sand and stain, and final inspection, is applied with the specific wood type in mind at every stage rather than treated as a fixed script. faq.q: How can I tell if my deck is cedar or pressure-treated?
faq.a: Cedar is generally softer, warmer in tone, and lighter in weight, while pressure-treated lumber often has a slight greenish tint when new and is denser. If you are unsure, send photos through /contact and it can be identified as part of your quote.

faq.q: Does cedar or pressure-treated wood hold stain longer?
faq.a: Both hold up well on a normal 2 to 4 year re-stain cycle when properly prepped. Cedar often shows a richer, more even colour, while pressure-treated wood's durability depends more on how thoroughly the fuzzy grain was managed during sanding.

faq.q: Can pressure-treated and cedar boards on the same deck be stained together?
faq.a: Yes. If a deck combines materials from a partial rebuild or added features, the process accounts for both wood types so the finished colour and protection are consistent across the whole structure.

faq.q: Why does my pressure-treated deck feel rough after sanding?
faq.a: Pressure-treated lumber can raise a fuzzy grain during sanding due to how the wood fibres respond to the treatment process. A proper sanding technique addresses this before staining so the finish lays down smoothly.

faq.q: Is soft washing only used on cedar decks?
faq.a: Soft washing is most commonly used on cedar because of its softer fibre, but it can also be the right choice for older or more fragile pressure-treated wood, depending on condition.

faq.q: Does the stain colour look different on cedar versus pressure-treated wood?
faq.a: Yes, slightly. Cedar's natural grain and tone often produce a richer look under transparent and semi-transparent stains, while pressure-treated wood can show more variation depending on how evenly it absorbs the finish.
